```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 5, fig.height = 5)
```

```{r setup}
library(HrankdCov)
```

## Motivation

Given an i.i.d. sample $(X_1, Y_1), \dots, (X_n, Y_n)$ of a pair of random
vectors $X \in \mathbb{R}^p$ and $Y \in \mathbb{R}^q$, we want to test
$H_0$: $X$ and $Y$ are independent.

* The distance covariance test (Székely, Rizzo and Bakirov, 2007) is
  consistent against all alternatives with finite first moments, but its
  null distribution depends on the unknown distributions of $X$ and $Y$, so
  that it requires permutation, and its power can suffer under heavy tails.
* For $p = q = 1$, applying a dependence measure to ranks gives tests that
  are *distribution-free*: the null distribution is the same for all
  continuous distributions.  Applying univariate ranks coordinate by
  coordinate does not achieve this when $p > 1$ or $q > 1$, because the
  joint distribution of the coordinatewise ranks of $X$ still depends on the
  dependence among the coordinates of $X$.

Center-outward ranks and signs (Hallin, del Barrio, Cuesta-Albertos and
Matrán, 2021) solve this problem.  Combining them with distance covariance
gives tests that are both distribution-free and consistent (Shi, Drton and
Han, 2022), and with score functions efficient ones (Shi, Hallin, Drton and
Han, 2022).  This package implements these tests.

## Center-outward ranks

The sample is matched to a grid of $n$ points in the unit ball by the
assignment that minimizes the total squared distance between the data and
the grid points.  The grid consists of $n_R$ spheres with radii
$1/(n_R+1), \dots, n_R/(n_R+1)$ intersected with $n_S$ rays, plus $n_0$
points close to the origin, where $n = n_R n_S + n_0$.  The grid is
symmetric about the origin: the rays come in antipodal pairs, and the extra
points are antipodal pairs at radius $1/(2(n_R+1))$, plus the origin when
$n_0$ is odd.

```{r grid}
g <- co_grid(300, 2)
attributes(g)[c("n_R", "n_S", "n_0")]
```

The matched grid point $F_\pm^{(n)}(X_i)$ is the value of the empirical
center-outward distribution function at $X_i$.  Its distance to the origin
gives the *center-outward rank* $R_\pm^{(n)}(X_i) = (n_R + 1)\|F_\pm^{(n)}(X_i)\|$
and its direction the *center-outward sign* $S_\pm^{(n)}(X_i)$.

```{r ranks}
set.seed(1)
n <- 300
z <- rnorm(n)
x <- cbind(z, z^2 + rnorm(n, sd = 0.5))   # a banana-shaped distribution
r <- co_ranks(x, n_R = 6)
r
```

Coloring the observations by their rank shows the empirical center-outward
quantile contours, which adapt to the shape of the distribution:

```{r ranks-plot}
plot(r, main = "Center-outward ranks")
```

In dimension one, center-outward ranks are the usual ranks folded at the
median: they measure how far an observation lies from the center.

```{r ranks-1d}
z <- c(2.3, -0.4, 0.1, 5.0, -1.2)
co_ranks(z)$F[, 1]
co_ranks(z)$rank
```

## Testing independence

`hrank_dcov_test()` computes the distance covariance of the center-outward
ranks of the two samples:

```{r test}
set.seed(2)
n <- 300
x <- matrix(rnorm(2 * n), ncol = 2)
y <- cbind(cos(2 * x[, 1]), x[, 2]^2) + matrix(rnorm(2 * n, sd = 0.5), ncol = 2)
hrank_dcov_test(x, y)
```

The dependence here is non-monotone and invisible to correlation
coefficients, yet it is detected.  The test is valid however heavy the tails
are, here with Cauchy-distributed observations:

```{r cauchy}
x_cauchy <- matrix(rt(2 * n, df = 1), ncol = 2)
y_cauchy <- matrix(rt(3 * n, df = 1), ncol = 3)
hrank_dcov_test(x_cauchy, y_cauchy)
```

### Score functions

Following Shi, Hallin, Drton and Han (2022), the ranks can be transformed by
a score function $J$ before computing the distance covariance, which replaces
$F_\pm^{(n)}(X_i)$ by $J(\|F_\pm^{(n)}(X_i)\|) S_\pm^{(n)}(X_i)$.  The
built-in choices are `"rank"` (Wilcoxon scores, $J(u) = u$, the default),
`"normal"` (van der Waerden scores, $J(u) = \sqrt{F^{-1}_{\chi^2_d}(u)}$)
and `"sign"` ($J(u) = 1$).  Normal scores often give more power for
light-tailed data:

```{r scores}
hrank_dcov_test(x, y, score = "normal")$p.value
hrank_dcov_test(x, y, score = "sign")$p.value
```

Any nonnegative function on $[0, 1)$ can be supplied as well, for example
`score = function(u) u^2`.  Use `co_scores()` to obtain the scored ranks.

## The null distribution

Under independence, the two rank vectors are independent and uniformly
distributed over the permutations of their grids.  The null distribution of
the statistic therefore depends only on $n$, $p$, $q$, the grids and the score
function.  Two ways of computing it are available.

* `method = "permutation"` (default) draws `B` random permutations.  The
  resulting p-value is exact in finite samples.
* `method = "asymptotic"` uses the limiting distribution
  $\sum_{k,l} \lambda_k \mu_l (\xi_{kl}^2 - 1)$ with independent standard
  normal $\xi_{kl}$ (Shi, Drton and Han, 2022).  The weights are the
  eigenvalues of the limiting kernel, computed by reducing the rotation
  invariant eigenvalue problem to one-dimensional radial integral equations
  via spherical harmonics; the tail probabilities are then obtained by
  Imhof's method, without any resampling.  The resulting critical values
  agree with those tabulated by Shi, Drton and Han (2022).  In moderate
  samples the test tends to be slightly conservative.

```{r null}
set.seed(3)
perm <- hrank_dcov_null(n, 2, 2, B = 1999)
asym <- hrank_dcov_null(n, 2, 2, method = "asymptotic")
rbind(permutation = quantile(perm), asymptotic = quantile(asym))
```

Because the null distribution does not depend on the data, it only needs to
be computed once for any number of tests with the same $n$, $p$ and $q$.
This is useful in simulation studies.  For example, the empirical size of
the test with Cauchy data and 200 replications:

```{r size}
set.seed(4)
pvals <- replicate(200, {
  x <- matrix(rt(2 * n, df = 1), ncol = 2)
  y <- matrix(rt(2 * n, df = 1), ncol = 2)
  hrank_dcov_test(x, y, null = asym)$p.value
})
mean(pvals <= 0.05)
```

The object returned by `hrank_dcov_test()` also contains the null
distribution it used, in its `null` component.

## Choice of the grid

By default, the grid has $n_R = \lfloor n^{1/4} \rfloor$ radii, as in Shi,
Drton and Han (2022), and its directions are deterministic: equally spaced on
the circle when $d = 2$, and given by a low-discrepancy sequence projected
onto the sphere when $d \ge 3$.  With `type = "random"`, the directions are
drawn uniformly at random instead.  Any data-independent choice gives a
distribution-free test; the number of radii can be changed with `n_R`.

```{r grid-options}
hrank_dcov(x, y, n_R = 5)
hrank_dcov(x, y, n_R = c(5, 10))
```

## References

Hallin, M., del Barrio, E., Cuesta-Albertos, J. and Matrán, C. (2021).
Distribution and quantile functions, ranks and signs in dimension d: A measure
transportation approach. *The Annals of Statistics*, 49(2), 1139--1165.

Shi, H., Drton, M. and Han, F. (2022). Distribution-free consistent
independence tests via center-outward ranks and signs. *Journal of the
American Statistical Association*, 117(537), 395--410.

Shi, H., Hallin, M., Drton, M. and Han, F. (2022). On universally consistent
and fully distribution-free rank tests of vector independence. *The Annals of
Statistics*, 50(4), 1933--1959.

Székely, G. J., Rizzo, M. L. and Bakirov, N. K. (2007). Measuring and testing
dependence by correlation of distances. *The Annals of Statistics*, 35(6),
2769--2794.
